transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-12-01
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Rajat Malhotra (Luminex Head of ML), Sana Kaur (Luminex Platform), Ethan Cole (CTO)
---
Summary (auto): POC scope for inference serving; focus on workload sizing, qps, concurrency, token distributions; action items to share traces and run benchmark.

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Avery from Redwood, I'll kick us off. Diego and I are here. How's everything over there, Rajat?
[00:12] Rajat: Hey, yeah thanks. We're excited. We basically want to get a POC scoped to validate cost and latency for our document ingestion pipeline and a chat assistant.
[00:22] Diego: Awesome. Can you walk us through the two main workloads you mentioned again - the doc ingestion embeddings and the real-time chat?
[00:30] Rajat: Sure. For embeddings we have batch jobs across nightly windows, about 200k docs per day, each document averages 800 tokens, but we chunk them so average request is 350 tokens input producing a 1536-d embedding, so big output but single vector. For chat, it's product-facing assistant - expected QPS around 12-15 at peak, concurrency maybe 80 to 120 concurrent sessions, typical user messages are short, like 20 to 120 input tokens, and responses average 150 to 300 tokens.
[01:10] Sana: Just to add, our peak is during US business hours, 13:00 to 17:00 UTC, and we have an SLA goal of 300ms generator latency for interactive flows. 300ms tail would be ideal but realistic is 500ms.
[01:25] Diego: Okay that's helpful. Two quick clarifications: when you say QPS 12-15 is that per endpoint or aggregated across regions?
[01:32] Rajat: That's per primary region (us-east), we also have secondary region for DR that sees maybe 10% of traffic.
[01:38] Ethan: And for the embeddings, we don't need strict tail latency, throughput and cost per vector is the main metric.
[01:45] Avery: Great. Let's outline success criteria - what would make the POC successful for you?
[01:52] Rajat: Three things: 1) latency for chat meet our SLO of p95 < 500ms for median flows; 2) cost estimate per 1MM tokens aligns with our projections (within 15%); 3) integration with our VPC and KMS without sending PII to public endpoints.
[02:08] Diego: Good. For the POC we'll run two bench types: synthetic steady-state QPS to validate latency at configured concurrency, and realistic replay using traces you provide to check token distribution and caching effects.
[02:20] Rajat: We can share call traces and an anonymized sample of payloads from the app, yes.
[02:26] Sana: I'll need to confirm what we can share re: payloads but we can definitely provide histogram of input/output token lengths and QPS samples.
[02:35] Avery: Awesome. Diego can you walk through the benchmark harness and what inputs we need?
[02:40] Diego: Sure. We use a harness that supports: variable QPS and concurrency; token-length sampling from distributions (you can provide percentiles); support for streaming vs non-streaming responses; and the ability to pin model variants. For embeddings we also need batch sizes and a note if you use async bulk ingestion.
[03:00] Rajat: For embeddings we do batches of 128 most of the time, but we also have a few legacy jobs that do 512.
[03:07] Diego: Perfect. For the chat workload to hit your p95 target we'll test with both streaming and non-streaming, because streaming changes tail behavior. Also we'll exercise prefix caching for repeated context - do you expect many repeated system prompts?
[03:22] Rajat: Yes, about 30% of chats share a common system prompt plus template personalization. So cache hit rate could be meaningful.
[03:30] Avery: On the infra side, can you confirm whether you want Redwood hosted or private VPC deployment for the POC?
[03:36] Ethan: For the POC we're open to Redwood-hosted but with VPC peering, ideally private control plane with customer-managed KMS. If that's not possible, a dedicated tenancy in Redwood hosted environment with envelope encryption is okay.
[03:50] Diego: We can do either. For private deployments we have a private control plane option and on-prem for enterprise, but POC usually starts hosted with VPC peering or dedicated nodes so we can get quick results.
[04:00] Sana: KMS integration details - we currently use AWS KMS and require HSM-backed CMKs for production, but POC can use standard KMS if we have proper audit logs.
[04:12] Avery: We'll share SOC2 and audit log capabilities. For the POC we'd propose: 1 week to set up infra and peering, 1 week to run benchmarks (1k synthetic + replay), then 1 week to analyze and present results. So roughly 3 weeks end-to-end. Does that timeline work?
[04:28] Rajat: That aligns with our internal decision cadence. We need results before our budget sync mid-Dec.
[04:35] Diego: Ok noted. Let's dig into traffic modeling — Rajat, can you give percentiles for token distribution?
[04:41] Rajat: Yes. For chat inputs: p50=45 tokens, p75=82, p90=140, p95=210. Outputs: p50=120, p75=180, p90=260, p95=340. Embedding chunk inputs p50=320, p75=410, p90=580.
[05:05] Diego: Great. For concurrency mapping we usually translate expected concurrent sessions and average think time to effective concurrency for the model. If you have 100 concurrent sessions with average user think time 35s and average model response time 0.5s, the model concurrency demand is roughly (QPS * latency). Do you have measured think times?
[05:22] Rajat: Our analytics show mean think time around 30-40s, yes.
[05:28] Diego: So that means the model concurrency for the chat path is mostly driven by user think time and QPS. We'll model with variable arrival patterns and also an occasional spike to 2x.
[05:38] Avery: We'll prepare a workload characterization doc to map your histogram to synthetic distributions the harness can consume.
[05:45] Rajat: When you say spikes, how do you handle autoscaling and warm KV cache? We worry about cold-start tails.
[05:53] Diego: Good question. Our runtime supports fast warm-up via prewarming of model instances and intelligent request routing; we also have short-term burst capacity if using Dedicated. For hosted, pre-warm policies can ensure low cold tail for your expected peak windows. We'll capture p99 tail in the benchmark.
[06:09] Sana: We need transparency on per-token billing and what counts as input vs output tokens. Also if we enable streaming does that change token accounting?
[06:17] Avery: Billing is per input and output tokens; streaming doesn't change token accounting but may influence latency profiles and effective cost if you hold connections open longer. We'll include cost model calc in the SOW.
[06:27] Ethan: On the competitor note — we've been testing Anthropic internally and OpenAI hosted for some flows. Cost vs latency tradeoffs are the main drivers. Would Redwood provide quantized model options?
[06:38] Diego: Yes we recommend quantized model variants for cost-sensitive workloads; during the POC we'll bench both full-precision and quantized variants and report quality delta.
[06:48] Rajat: For quality metric we'll use perplexity on a dev set and a small human eval set for the assistant responses.
[06:55] Avery: Good — we'll need the dev set and a few golden prompts for human eval. Rajat, can you provide those?
[07:01] Rajat: yes we can. I'll work with our ML team.
[07:05] Diego: Now, specific benchmark numbers we'll collect: p50/p95/p99 latency for single-turn and multi-turn, throughput (tokens/s), cost per 1M tokens, cache hit rate effect, and embedding throughput and cost per vector.
[07:18] Sana: Do you simulate multi-turn stateful sessions to evaluate KV cache sizing?
[07:22] Diego: Yes the harness simulates user sessions and manages contexts; we can measure KV cache hit rate and memory footprint under concurrency.
[07:29] Rajat: What's the logging and audit capability — we need to capture request IDs and full audit logs without payloads for compliance.
[07:36] Avery: We can provide audit logs and request-level tracing; for PII we'll configure redaction and send only metadata for auditing. We'll also support customer-managed retention policies.
[07:46] Ethan: For the VPC peering, can you walk through networking requirements briefly?
[07:50] Diego: We'll need a peering connection and a couple firewall rules; for private deployments, there'll be an initial infra checklist including subnet ranges, KMS ARNs, and service account IP whitelisting. We'll send a template.
[08:03] Rajat: Regarding success criteria, can you include cost sensitivity bands? E.g. if cost is >20% above our target it's a fail.
[08:11] Avery: Yes we'll codify pass/fail bands in the SOW: latency pass if p95 < 500ms, cost pass if within 15% of projection, security pass if KMS + VPC peering validated and audit logs enabled.
[08:22] Diego: On modeling QPS, we'll run three synthetic scenarios: baseline (12 QPS), peak (30 QPS spike), and bursty (2x short window). We'll also replay your traces to get realistic patterns.
[08:33] Rajat: For embeddings has to be able to support our nightly peak of 200k docs — how do you model that?
[08:39] Diego: We'll convert docs/day into sustained throughput during the nightly window; if you batch 128, 200k docs is ~1,563 batches — we'll test throughput and measure GPU utilization, and recommend batching/quantization profiles to hit cost targets.
[08:53] Sana: Are there recommended GPUs for embeddings vs chat? We use mixed workloads.
[08:58] Diego: For embeddings, dense GPU with high memory and good matrix throughput matters; for chat low latency, A100-like profiles or inference-optimized SKUs are ideal. We'll include recommended SKU mapping in the POC report.
[09:10] Rajat: For the replay tests we'll need to ensure tokens are anonymized and can't be reconstructed — is that okay on your side?
[09:17] Avery: Yes we can sign an NDA addendum if needed and will accept anonymized traces. We'll also support an on-prem option if data cannot leave your network.
[09:26] Ethan: One more on timelines — you mentioned 3 weeks earlier; can we compress if we do hosted + limited scope?
[09:32] Avery: We can compress to 2 weeks if you accept Redwood-hosted dedicated nodes and provide traces quickly. That reduces infra setup time.
[09:40] Rajat: We can try to meet that. Our internal deadline is 2026-12-15 for the budget sync.
[09:47] Diego: Great. I'll outline the benchmark plan and inputs we need: token histograms, QPS time series for a week, sample payloads (anonymized), and dev set for quality checks.
[09:58] Rajat: We'll aim to share those by end of week.
[10:02] Avery: Okay last bit — do you have any regulatory or residency constraints?
[10:07] Sana: No strict residency, but logs and KMS must stay in our AWS account; certification SOC2 is required, FedRAMP not required.
[10:16] Avery: Perfect. We'll include SOC2 documentation. Diego, anything else on the technical checklist?
[10:22] Diego: I'll include the harness config, the model variants we'll test, quantization profiles, and the telemetry we'll collect (latency percentiles, GPU utilization, token throughput, cost per token).
[10:33] Avery: Cool. Let's recap next steps...
[10:36] Rajat: Quick question — will you support function-calling or structured outputs in the assistant POC? We use structured JSON responses for downstream pipelines.
[10:44] Diego: Yes we support function/tool calling; we'll validate structured output formats during quality tests.
[10:49] Avery: Recap / Next steps: 1) Redwood to send SOW and pricing (Avery) by 2026-12-03; 2) Redwood to send benchmark harness and infra checklist (Diego) by 2026-12-04; 3) Luminex to share token histograms, sample payloads, and dev set (Rajat/Sana) by 2026-12-04; 4) Run benchmark week of 2026-12-08 targeted.
[11:12] Rajat: Sounds good. We'll set up a calendar invite for infra sync.
[11:16] Avery: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with artifacts.
[11:20] Ethan: Thanks all.
[11:22] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional transcription errors present (e.g., KMS heard as 'KMSs' or 'kms'), and speaker labels may differ slightly in Fireflies export.
